records.name: Benin
records.summary: Benin is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but 76crimes documents that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace; the Hirondelles Club provides safe housing for LGBT youth fleeing family violence. No LGR, no anti-discrimination law; community organises underground.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (9 Apr 2024): the Hirondelles Club at Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth in Benin since about 2020 — a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; the report's framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. For this record: the current statutory baseline — legal but entirely unshielded, no recognition pathway.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. For this record: official US assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. For this record: regional religious-institution hostility including Benin — dated 2015, treat as context not current-state evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

freshness.fact: Adult same-sex acts legal; art.545 (2018 code) adds penalties for acts with minors; strong social hostility and lynchings; 2023 US State picture holds.

records.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
records.summary:
These are not autonomous countries but special municipalities of the kingdom itself, so metropolitan equality law applies directly: same-sex marriage has been performed on the islands since 2012 — one small island hosted the region's first such wedding after the 2010 status change and markets civil ceremonies openly — with the state's penal-code discrimination grounds and partnership frameworks in force, and a current-status review confirming no later change.

The caveats are the kingdom's own, and they are real: legal gender change still requires a medical expert's statement (the self-declaration act was withdrawn at kingdom level in July 2025), non-binary markers demand months-long court procedure, and three tiny church-dense communities leave service depth thin — the same rights overview that documents these gaps rates them with the metropolitan standard attached. Travel-side evidence is warm and wedding-positive; no adverse enforcement is documented.

sources.claim: GayCities (14 Dec 2022, updated 1 Sep 2023): 'Top 10 destinations that celebrate marriage equality in the Caribbean and Latin America' ranks Bonaire at #5 — as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are protected by strict anti-discrimination laws, same-sex couples are warmly welcomed; notes Bonaire uses the US dollar. For this record: travel-facing evidence that the island markets itself as equality-friendly with statutory protection behind it.

Dutch Caribbean Legal Portal (5 Dec 2012): the Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union — Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27) on 4 Dec 2012, two visiting residents. For this record: same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012, and the territory has a track record of performing them for visitors.

Saba Tourism official weddings page: the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony is the Court Room in the Administrative Building; registrar Julieta Woods is documented as flexible with couples' wishes; full destination-wedding infrastructure (caterers, flowers, accommodations). For this record: practical logistics for a couple — civil ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry.

freshness.fact: Dutch equality law applies to the public bodies; same-sex marriage performed on Bonaire/Sint Eustatius/Saba since 2018; no later change found.

records.name: Burkina Faso
records.summary:
Burkina Faso is dangerous for trans visitors. In July 2024 the military junta approved a revised Personal and Family Code criminalising homosexuality — Burkina Faso had never previously outlawed it. The junta (Traoré) has clamped down on opposition and media, promised elections have not been held, and much of the country faces jihadist insurgency. Enforcement details of the new law remain unclear (HDT notes drafting uncertainty), but the direction and the absence of any institutional recourse are unambiguous.

For a visitor: new criminalisation under a junta, plus severe general security conditions.

sources.claim: BBC (11 July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta announced a ban on homosexual acts — homosexuality had never before been outlawed in the socially conservative West African state; part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage/family law. SUPERSEDED: the ban entered into force as criminal-code law on 1 Sep 2025. For this record: the decisive policy-reversal date, later confirmed in force.

Africanews (11 Jul 2024, updated 13 Aug 2024): the junta's council approved a decree for a new Personal and Family Code (CPF) that 'enshrines the ban on homosexuality', per a presidency statement, joining the ~22 of 54 African states disallowing same-sex relations. SUPERSEDED: entered into force 1 Sep 2025. For this record: legislative vehicle and date for the criminalisation.

Human Rights Watch (3 Sep 2025): the Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the law on 1 September 2025 making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence — two to five years' imprisonment plus fines — enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space. For this record: the operative criminalisation date and penalties; core current-state evidence.

LGBTQ Nation (Sep 2025): the junta unanimously passed the law; Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala states prison 'between two and five years as well as fines' for perpetrators of 'homosexual or similar practices', and that foreigners will be DEPORTED under the law; junta rule since Sep 2022. For this record: penalties plus explicit deportation exposure for foreign nationals — directly visitor-relevant.

freshness.fact: New criminal code in force 1 Sep 2025 criminalises same-sex acts and 'promotion' of homosexuality (junta bill of Jul 2024) — previously legal. Sharply worse.

records.name: Bangladesh
records.summary:
Bangladesh is a dangerous destination for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport.

The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (12 Feb 2025): prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work. For this record: lethal violence against visible trans people continues — case specifics (Rangamati, Feb 2025).

Erasing 76 Crimes (7 Apr 2026) citing JMBF's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — 'a sharp increase' continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder/attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. For this record: the current national incident baseline — magnitude and trend for a visitor assessing exposure.

Global Press Journal: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding. For this record: the 2024 regime-change inflection point where formal rights began rolling back in practice.

Washington Blade (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's ouster (August 2024), Bangladesh's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. For this record: a dated, post-coup security assessment directly relevant to a visitor's risk calculus.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Bangladesh (September 2023, updated April 2026): Section 377 ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within s.377 (ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to 'all genders'). For this record: authoritative statement of the legal ambiguity any visitor's conduct sits inside.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Penal Code 1860 criminalises 'intercourse against the order of nature' with up to life imprisonment — rarely enforced but used by police to harass people presumed LGBTIQ; hijra are legally recognised as a third gender since 2014 with gender-marker change allowed; LGBTIQ and hijra pride events have been held. For this record: the legal baseline plus the harassment-not-prosecution enforcement pattern and third-gender recognition.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Oct 2025): after hijras refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles in Narayanganj — a traditional livelihood. For this record: extortion-driven police violence against visibly trans people, including disruption of street livelihoods.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Apr 2024): five transgender/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, per JMBF. For this record: policing of visibly trans people concentrates at transit hubs — the airport itself is a documented hotspot.

UK Upper Tribunal decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal — Home Office country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues (citing fact-finding missions and IRB Canada). For this record: asylum-grade evidence of state-tolerated hostility; international-regime (asylum) source in scope by design.

freshness.fact: Section 377 ambiguity persists (life imprisonment for 'unnatural offences'); hijra third gender since 2014; five men caned Apr 2026 — enforcement continues.

records.name: Bulgaria
records.summary:
Bulgaria is workable for trans visitors — an EU member with no traveler-facing restrictions, but one of the EU's most hostile social climates. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The European Court of Justice is actively hearing the Shipov case on Bulgaria's refusal to issue ID matching lived gender, and EU free-movement law provides a legal backstop.

The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the Supreme Court of Cassation ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (gender an "unchangeable biological factor"), parliament passed a Russia-style law banning "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools (August 2024), and the EU's FRA survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above EU averages. Hate speech by politicians is routine.

For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and Sofia has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic.

sources.claim: Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004 (direct and indirect — housing, education, medication) expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex' including 'sex change'. For this record: the current statutory baseline — old decriminalisation, layered but incomplete protection.

DW (Sep 2025): ECJ Advocate General Richard de la Tour issued an opinion that EU law as interpreted precludes national legislation like Bulgaria's refusing a trans person ID documents matching presented gender — the court concurred with the AG's proposed reasoning. For this record: EU-law pressure to overturn Bulgaria's legal-recognition ban — dated Sep 2025, pending full judgment.

Strasbourg Observers (17 Dec 2024) on Y.T. v Bulgaria: the original 2020 ECtHR judgment found an Article 8 violation over refusal of legal gender recognition, and the Court made clear those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 registry revision (consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria); Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic. For this record: the legal explanation for Bulgaria's recognition ban and its continuing unlawfulness.

Amnesty International (Feb 2015, 'Missing the point'): authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes — legislation exists but bias attacks (spiking in 2013 per the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee) go unpursued; Sofia Prosecution opened some cases. For this record: institutional non-response to bias crime — dated but establishes the pattern later reports inherit.

Human Rights Watch (5 Jun 2017): urges authorities to protect the 10 June Sofia Pride march, noting a group called the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse Sofia from garbage'. For this record: organised far-right hostility to visible LGBT events — dated evidence of the threat environment around public LGBT visibility.

Novinite (June 2011): the 4th annual Sofia Pride parade passed without incidents under heavy police guard, drawing only a 'Family NGO' protest — after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. For this record: historical baseline of pride security dynamics (protection-dependent order).

records.name: Bahrain
records.summary:
Bahrain is a place to avoid entirely, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the Gulf. Uniquely among Gulf states, same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976, and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression. The UK foreign office notes "arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare."

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A Brazilian trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker. In 2023 a court rejected a trans man's recognition application citing Islamic Sharia, and in February 2024 the lower house of parliament adopted a bill to criminalise "acts of deviance" — a deteriorating trajectory.

For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment.

sources.claim: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Bahrain' (continuously updated): legal status 'decriminalised since 1976' per ILGA-sourced infobox, with recognition limits and no SOGIESC discrimination protections. For this record: tertiary overview consistent with the Outright/State Department baseline — orientation source only, not stand-alone evidence.

Cairo 52 (7 Feb 2024): in a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia — including refusal of a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested. For this record: the documented judicial-refusal practice blocking legal transition at first instance.

Cairo 52 country review: Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade — including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International — so local media often serve as the only source. For this record: an evidence-reliability caveat — most findings for this jurisdiction rest on thin, partly remote sourcing.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era law, and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy — but authorities still use 'indecency' and 'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people (the Feb 2024 Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation). For this record: decriminalisation with the residual-arrest pattern — the nuance a visitor's safety turns on.

Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada RIO BHR105575.E (Aug 2016, covering 2011–Jul 2016): reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain' (citing Canada 14 Jul 2016 and Gulf News 5 Feb 2011) plus societal-attitude and treatment-by-authorities research. For this record: a SOURCE CONFLICT — this contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading of Wikipedia/Outright/2023 US State Dept; treat as unresolved, flagged for intake follow-up rather than ground truth.

freshness.fact: Consensual same-sex conduct not criminalised (2023 US State); courts since 2023 reject gender-affirming procedures; legal gender recognition still denied.

records.name: Bahamas
records.summary: The Bahamas demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 1991; tourism-dependent economy with extensive international exposure; no LGR; documented social hostility but no criminalisation and no police-targeting pattern.

sources.claim: The Tribune (27 Apr 2016): Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign; BTIU stressed there are no laws protecting transgender and intersex Bahamians, and member Torri Culmer advocates against job termination for trans/intersex workers. For this record: documented absence of trans-specific legal protection plus organised advocacy.

GayLawNet Bahamas law page: on 16 May 1991 consensual same-sex sex was decriminalised (Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act), and in May 1998 the National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced the military, prison service and police do not discriminate. For this record: the statutory decriminalisation date plus an official non-discrimination statement.

The Tribune (8 May 2017): Adrian Brown, 24 (Jamaica-born, US-resident), was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being 'targeted and beat up' because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early Saturday, and wants charges laid. For this record: violent targeting of a gay VISITOR during a major tourist event — direct visitor-risk evidence, dated 2017.

freshness.fact: Male acts decriminalised 1991, no recent legal change; social homophobia prominent (Dec 2018 Canadian travel advice) — still the tourist climate.

records.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
records.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; Sarajevo Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress. Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report: negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in Republika Srpska and rural areas.

sources.claim: Sarajevo Open Centre, Pink Report 2024 (13 Jun 2024): annual report on LGBTI human rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina — the past year saw a number of negative events with significant impact, and the long-visible worsening trend is 'becoming increasingly evident'. For this record: current national climate assessment from the leading local monitor.

Balkan Diskurs (25 Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice — the Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on 'completed' medical transition, constraints described as discriminatory and degrading. For this record: the documentation pathway a trans person navigating the system faces — resident-facing, not a border issue.

Human Rights Watch (4 Feb 2014): violent attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers — Sarajevo Open Centre staff said they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier; HRW's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of attackers. For this record: precedent that organised anti-LGBT violence occurs even WITH prior police coordination (dated 2014, context for later attacks).

GlobalGayz (2012): same-sex conduct decriminalised in the Federation of BiH (1996) and Republika Srpska (1998) via the two entities' own criminal codes; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation but omitted gender identity as originally intended. For this record: entity-level legal baseline plus the pre-2016 gender-identity protection gap.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): BiH's amended Anti-Discrimination Law explicitly covers sexual orientation and gender identity with correct local terminology — SOC co-presented the amendments with the Agency for Gender Equality after fall-2015 public consultations. For this record: the statutory protection now on the books at state level.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): the Federation of BiH adopted hate-crime regulation explicitly naming sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances — SOC coordinator Vladana Vasić confirming the long-sought coalition win. For this record: entity-level sentencing enhancement for bias attacks in FBiH (RS runs its own separate regime).

freshness.fact: Legal state-wide (1996/98/2003); entities restrict marriage to opposite-sex couples; uneven protections, 2023 activist attack; ILGA-2024 picture stands.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina
